source: Rayner, Li, Williams, Cave and Well (2007) Eye movements during information processing tasks: individual differences and cultural effects
finding: Gap 5. A direct test of Chua 2005 with more scenes. Across all scenes Chinese did not look longer at background or shorter at foreground. On the 6 scenes most like Chua's (one or two clear focal objects) part of the effect appeared.
numbers: N=74 recruited in 3 groups (24 native English, 23 native Chinese, rest bilingual). All scenes: background time Chinese 2489 ms vs American 2565 ms, F<1; foreground 6445 vs 6633 ms, p>.10; group x fixation-order interaction F<1. Six Chua-like scenes: foreground 4299 vs 4813 ms, t(45)=2.10, p=.04; background fixations 16.3 vs 13.8, t(45)=2.34, p=.02; background time 4346 vs 4183 ms, t<1; group x area interaction F(1,45)=2.26 p=.14 (time), 2.08 p=.16 (count). Chinese had shorter and more numerous fixations on faces and scenes, mostly a trade-off.
quote: there was no evidence that Chinese participants spent more time looking at the background information
limits: Stimulus-dependent. Subset tests are post hoc and the interaction was not significant. Native Chinese in the US, student samples. Authors say fixation-duration differences relate to writing-system experience more than culture.
agent_relevance: Background attention differences depend on scene design; a boundary-condition result, not a stable trait.

source: Rayner, Castelhano and Yang (2009) Eye movements when looking at unusual/weird scenes: are there cultural differences?
finding: Gap 5. No cultural difference in how fast or long Americans and Chinese fixated an odd object, or in whole-scene measures.
numbers: N=24 (12 American, 12 native Chinese), 20 scene sets, normal vs weird. All group effects and group interactions F<1. Whole scene: fixation duration Chinese 282/281 ms vs American 280/284 ms (normal/weird); total viewing 4108/4152 vs 4182/4198 ms. Time to ROI fixation 1415 vs 1352 ms (normal), 1270 vs 1257 (weird). Authors cite Evans et al. (in press) as a second null.
quote: no evidence of any cultural differences while viewing either scene type
limits: Small N, but all F<1 and CIs reported. Tests oddity capture, not the Chua focal-object measure.
agent_relevance: Two independent labs found nulls on the same culture-attention claim; keep the eye-level claim contested.

source: Goh, Tan and Park (2009) Culture modulates eye-movements to visual novelty
finding: Pro-effect evidence from a third lab. Americans fixated objects and backgrounds longer; Singaporean Chinese moved gaze more between objects and background. Both groups responded to object change.
numbers: N=31 (16 US, 15 Chinese Singaporean). Object fixation duration 254.2 vs 170.3 ms, F(1,29)=8.09, eta2=.22. Background fixation duration 220.6 vs 151.6 ms, F(1,29)=7.67, eta2=.21. Gaze distance Singapore 710.2 vs US 477.2 px, F(1,29)=21.81, eta2=.43. Object-background gaze moves 8.0% vs 3.9%, F(1,29)=21.43, eta2=.43. Within-object moves US 69.1% vs 59.5%, F(1,29)=4.68, eta2=.14. Within-background moves: no culture effect. Implied d about 1.0 to 1.7.
limits: Small N, large effects, passive viewing, 50 Hz tracker, Singapore is a bilingual setting. Effects are mainly in dwell and dispersion.
agent_relevance: Effects this large from N=31 are likely inflated; not a design anchor.

source: Derived effect size for Chua, Boland and Nisbett (2005) first-fixation effect (computed from the t value read earlier)
finding: Gap 5. The 118 ms earlier object fixation, t(43)=2.41, equals about d=0.74, Hedges g=0.72, 95% CI about 0.12 to 1.33.
numbers: Computed here: d=2t/sqrt(df)=0.735; g=0.722; SE about 0.31 with n=21 and 24. For comparison Goh 2009 object-duration eta2=.22 implies d about 1.06. Rayner 2007 full-set differences are near zero.
limits: Derived by hand from reported t and group sizes. Lower CI bound is near 0. No formal meta-analysis of the eye-tracking effect was found.
agent_relevance: Treat the true effect as small to moderate and scene-dependent, not large.

source: Kelly, Jack, Miellet, De Luca, Foreman and Caldara (2011) Social experience does not abolish cultural diversity in eye movements
finding: Boundary condition (faces, not scenes): British-born Chinese mostly kept Eastern eye-movement strategies; about 25% showed Western ones. Culture alone does not explain it.
numbers: Majority of British Born Chinese adults used Eastern strategies; about 25% Western; strategy consistent across recognition and expression tasks within person.
agent_relevance: Individual strategy differences are large; supports not hard-coding cultural personas.

source: Gingras, Estephan, Fiset, Lingnan, Caldara and Blais (2023) Eye movements for face recognition: Canadian vs Chinese, not modulated by social orientation
finding: Cultural group differences in face fixations replicated, but priming individualism or collectivism did not change them, and questionnaire links were limited to some subdimensions.
numbers: Two experiments: priming paradigm (Exp 1) and two IND/COL questionnaires (Exp 2); group differences present; priming effect absent.
limits: Faces only. Tests a social-orientation mechanism for eye behaviour, which fails.
agent_relevance: If the cause is not social orientation, a collectivist role prompt is unlikely to be the right lever for attention style.

source: Lu, Song and Zhang (2025) Cultural tendencies in generative AI. Nature Human Behaviour
finding: Gap 7. Only the abstract was reachable (paywall; Europe PMC abstract). It claims GPT is more interdependent and holistic in Chinese than English, replicated in ERNIE; cultural role prompts adjust it.
numbers: No numbers obtainable. Abstract: GPT and ERNIE; social orientation and cognitive style; real-world test with advertisement recommendations.
limits: Full text and items not obtained. Items and prompts were not released, per Sun and Wang. Gap stays open for primary numbers.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on this result; the replication evidence is weaker.

source: Sun and Wang (2025) The fragility of cultural tendencies in LLMs, appendix critique of Lu et al.
finding: Gap 7. Critique of Lu et al.'s design: 4 to 12 test items across seven tasks, two models, items not released, only one of seven tasks used non-public items, prompt templates not shared. Sun and Wang call the original data statistically robust but not evidence of grounded cognition.
numbers: 4 to 12 items per task; 2 models (gpt, ernie); 1 of 7 tasks with non-public data. Their replication: Exp 1 language d=0.045 p=.150; framing d=-2.095, eta2=.54.
limits: Second-hand account of Lu. Sun and Wang could not use the exact items. The critics are not neutral.
agent_relevance: Memorisation of public scale items is a live explanation for the language effect.

source: Sabir et al. (2025) VLM captions holistic vs analytic: Table 6 caption-language control
finding: Gap 9. Partly crossed test on COCO captions: language of the caption text shifts the holistic share by roughly 11 to 15 points, while changing the image set from COCO to Japanese images shifts it about 47 points.
numbers: 5K captions, GPT-4o classifier 6-shot: English original 12.34% holistic vs Japanese machine-translated 27.54% (+15.2); Japanese original 27.48% vs English machine-translated 16.26% (+11.2); back-translations 15.20% and 26.58%. Average shift 13.21% after translation. GPT4o-JP: COCO 26.10% vs 1K Japanese photos 73.37% (+47.3).
limits: Not fully crossed in one model run; the content shift is for one captioner on different image sets. Judge is GPT-4o few-shot; human check on 200 COCO captions only (GPT4o-JP 17.75% holistic by humans vs 29.00% by GPT-4o).
agent_relevance: Content dominates, language is a smaller but real effect, and the judge inflates holistic share vs humans.

source: Sabir et al. (2025) Tables 2, 4 and 5: plain vs Japanese-tuned model on Japanese image sets
finding: Gap 9. On the 1K Japanese set plain GPT-4o already gives 57.6 to 59.1% holistic; the Japanese-tuned GPT4o-JP gives 63.86 to 73.37%. On COCO 1K the plain model gives 26.2%.
numbers: GPT4o 59.10 (5-shot) and 57.60 (balanced 6-shot) on 1K JP; GPT4o-JP 63.86 and 73.37; HERON-BENCH GPT4o 25.58/27.91 vs GPT4o-JP 34.88/53.49; JA-VLM 23.81/19.05 vs 38.10/61.90. COCO 1K: GPT4o 26.20, GPT4o-JP 35.50, VILA-JP 24.00. Human 200-caption check: VILA-JP 15.33% holistic, GPT4o-JP 17.75%.
limits: The 6-shot balanced arm changes the few-shot examples, so prompt design alone moves the share by up to 19 points (HERON GPT4o-JP 34.88 to 53.49).
agent_relevance: Few-shot example composition moves outputs as much as culture cues. Reinforces a wording control.

source: Jin et al. (2023) Cultural psychology of LLMs: is ChatGPT a holistic or analytic thinker? methods re-read for item count
finding: Gap 2. The triad test used 20 items, of which only half were real analysis/holism items and half were placeholders. Similarity matches coded analytic, relation matches coded holistic. Comparison was to Chinese provincial means, not a US norm.
numbers: TCT: 10 runs, mean relational share GPT-3.5 0.87 (SD 0.06), GPT-4 0.85 (SD 0.05), temperature 1 baseline. Both above most Chinese provinces.
limits: Real items are published triads (likely seen in training); no fresh-item control; about 10 effective items.
agent_relevance: Contamination of the relational-triad result is untested; treat as informational.

source: Hu et al. (2026) Cultural alignment multi-task LLM study, Task 4 triad item and scoring
finding: Gap 2. The triad prompt uses the textbook example 'Seagull, Sky, Dog' (Ji et al. 2004) and an R-C score where higher means relational. Under this scoring the US model is more relational than the Chinese model.
numbers: R-C: US model 8.10 (SD 1.44) vs Chinese 6.04 (SD 1.54), d=1.38; prompt language 7.10 vs 7.04.
limits: Different scoring and items than Jin; both likely contaminated by the famous example. No study with unseen triads found.
agent_relevance: Relational share is not stable across scoring and model; do not use it as a representation-bias claim.

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov and Suhr (2023) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design
finding: Gap 1. Meaning-preserving formatting changes alone change accuracy by up to 76 points for LLaMA-2-13B and about 10 points on average across 50+ tasks; not removed by model size, more shots, or instruction tuning.
numbers: Median spread 7.5 accuracy points across tasks; spreads over 70 points on some tasks; at least 15 points for all LLaMA-2 settings, 9 for Falcon; GPT-3.5 up to 56 points, median 6.4 across 320 formats.
limits: Formatting (separators, casing), not semantic wording like 'belongs to' vs 'is similar to'. Mostly open models, few-shot.
agent_relevance: Rough noise floor for any scaffold test: a gain under about 7 to 10 points can sit inside the wording spread. Supports a wording control in G7 tests.

source: Cao et al. (2024) On the worst prompt performance of LLMs (RobustAlpacaEval)
finding: Gap 1. Semantically equivalent rewrites of the same query give very different results; worst-prompt performance is far below the mean and prompt-engineering fixes help little.
numbers: Llama-2-70B-chat: worst-to-best difference 45.48%, worst performance as low as 9.38%.
limits: Open-ended instruction following judged by GPT-4, not reasoning accuracy. Older open models.
agent_relevance: Report worst and best over paraphrases, not one wording, when comparing scaffolds.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (GSM-IC)
finding: Gap 3. Closest tested analogue to 'focus on the object, ignore context': irrelevant sentences hurt, and a one-sentence instruction to ignore irrelevant information recovers a few points at nearly equal tokens.
numbers: code-davinci-002 micro accuracy: chain-of-thought 72.4 vs with 'feel free to ignore irrelevant information' 77.8 (+5.4); least-to-most 77.5 vs 80.6 (+3.1); zero-shot CoT 29.0 vs 30.5; program 54.4 vs 56.7. Only 18% of base problems solved across all distractor types.
limits: One 2023 model, math word problems, small gains. No 'attend to context first' arm was tested; the context-first direction is untested.
agent_relevance: Instruction framing gives a few points; a context-first vs focus-first test on our agent still needs to be run.

source: Gentner, Rattermann and Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: Gap 8. Retrieval from memory is driven by surface (object) similarity; judged soundness is driven by relational structure. Analogies are rated most sound yet recalled less than surface matches.
numbers: Exp 1 mean soundness (1 to 5): analogy 4.40, surface-similarity 2.80, first-order relations only 2.74. Quality of reminding: surface similarity 2.36 > analogy 1.48 > first-order relations 0.86, F(2,58)=72.81, p<.0001.
limits: Story reminding with students, 1993. Not a taxonomy-vs-theme study; relational cues help only when also object-similar.
agent_relevance: For O7, retrieval on shared relational structure will be weak unless surface cues are also present; test a cue that names the relation.

source: Search results (2026) analogical retrieval by LLMs: Jiayang et al. 2023 and ADR-bench, snippets
finding: Gap 8. Snippets only: LLMs are reported as distracted by surface similarity in analogy tasks (30% vs 85% for humans, per a 2026 citing paper) and LLM agents fail at structure-matching historical analogy retrieval.
numbers: 30% LLM vs 85% human accuracy (secondhand). Das and Balke (INLG 2025) four-way analogy benchmark shows limits in structured relational reasoning.
agent_relevance: Consistent with d16: surface cues dominate retrieval.

source: Search results (2026) LLMs on thematic vs taxonomic triads by child age
finding: Gap 6. A further search found no study that gives LLMs thematic vs taxonomic triads and compares with child age data. Human work shows a shift to taxonomic with age, but thematic and taxonomic choices both occur in 2-year-olds when task demands are low.
numbers: No LLM numbers exist. Human: preschoolers group thematically, older participants taxonomically (Ralli and Niasti, abstract level).
limits: Absence after one web search plus earlier searches; APIs rate-limited. Weak evidence of absence.
agent_relevance: Cheap experiment still open; low priority for the schema.

source: Uskul et al. (2008) Ecocultural basis of cognition: farmers and fishermen are more holistic than herders
finding: Boundary condition seen in a search listing only: holistic style tracks subsistence (farming, fishing) within one region, not East vs West.
agent_relevance: Style differences follow ecology and task, not region labels.
